blocks.text: The steel piles of a coastal jetty look sound above the tide line, yet a survey finds some piles with a hole through a 12 mm wall at mid-tide, while the bulk of the pile has lost less than 1 mm. The same ocean attacks the same steel in very different ways depending on where, and recognising the form of attack is the first step toward stopping it.

blocks.markdown: Corrosion is an electrochemical process (anodic metal dissolution paired with a cathodic reaction such as oxygen reduction). The *form* in which it appears depends on how the anodic and cathodic sites are arranged on the surface and on the environment. Four forms are essential in this unit: uniform, pitting, crevice and stress-corrosion cracking.

rows: Uniform
Even thinning of the whole exposed surface; rust or scale across the area
Carbon steel in air, soil, acids
Predictable; loss rate can be allowed for as a corrosion allowance
Pitting
Isolated small cavities, often deep, with the surrounding surface almost unattacked
Passive films broken locally, for example chloride on stainless steel or aluminium
Perforation with little overall mass loss
Crevice
Attack confined inside or at the mouth of a narrow gap, for example under a washer, gasket, deposit or lap joint
Stagnant electrolyte in a gap, oxygen depleted, chloride and acidity concentrated
Hidden damage at joints
Stress-corrosion cracking (SCC)
Fine, branching cracks with little metal loss and no visible warning
Tensile stress plus a specific environment plus a susceptible alloy, for example austenitic stainless steel in hot chloride, or brass in ammonia
Sudden brittle-looking fracture
blocks.caption: Four forms of corrosion distinguished by appearance.

blocks.title: Pitting factor
blocks.text: The pitting factor is the depth of the deepest pit divided by the average penetration calculated from mass loss: $\text{pitting factor}=d_{\max}/d_{\text{avg}}$. A value of 1 means uniform attack; large values mean a localised attack that could perforate the wall long before the bulk of the metal has gone.

blocks.markdown: **Pitting and crevice attack** share a self-sustaining mechanism. Inside a pit or crevice, metal dissolves and the dissolved ions hydrolyse, making the local solution acidic, while chloride ions migrate in to balance the positive charge. Oxygen cannot reach the inside, so the cathodic reaction happens on the large outer surface. The small anode area sees a large cathodic current, so the attack is fast and local. **Stress-corrosion cracking** needs three things together: a tensile stress (applied or residual), a specific corrosive environment and a susceptible alloy; removing any one prevents it.

blocks.title: Telling the forms apart
blocks.text: Ask three questions: Is the attack over the whole surface (uniform)? Is it localised in cavities on an open surface (pitting) or only within a gap (crevice)? Are there cracks with little metal loss, and was the part under tensile stress (SCC)? The location and shape of damage identify the mechanism and hence the remedy.

blocks.markdown: **Cathodic protection (CP)** makes the whole structure the cathode of a cell, so that metal dissolution is suppressed. For steel in seawater the usual criterion is a potential of about $-0.80$ V against an Ag/AgCl reference (typical protective value). It is achieved in two ways: a **sacrificial anode** (a more active metal such as zinc, aluminium alloy or magnesium that corrodes in place of the steel) and **impressed current** (an external DC rectifier driving current from inert anodes into the electrolyte and onto the structure).

rows: Power supply
None; driven by the galvanic potential difference
External DC rectifier needed
Anode
Zinc, aluminium alloy or magnesium; consumed and replaced
Inert (for example mixed-metal-oxide titanium, graphite); consumed very slowly
Current
Limited by the anode potential difference; fixed
Adjustable and large; can follow demand
Best for
Small or well-coated structures, short and medium life
Large structures, long life, high-resistivity electrolytes
Drawbacks
Anodes add weight and must be replaced
Needs power, monitoring and maintenance; overprotection can damage coatings or embrittle high-strength steel with hydrogen

blocks.title: Life of a zinc anode system
blocks.prompt: A coated steel structure has $A=200$ m$^2$ in seawater. The coating has a breakdown factor $f_b=0.10$ and bare steel needs a current density of $i_d=100$ mA m$^{-2}$ (assumed). Zinc anodes of total mass 300 kg, capacity 780 A h kg$^{-1}$ (typical practical value) and utilisation $u=0.85$ are fitted. Find the anode life.

steps.text: Current demand: only the broken-coating fraction of the area needs current.
Total charge available from the anodes, in ampere-hours, after allowing for utilisation.
Life is the charge divided by the current, then converted to years.

blocks.answer: About 99 500 h, or about 11.4 years, before the anodes are exhausted.

blocks.title: Impressed-current demand and power
blocks.prompt: A bare steel pier of submerged area 180 m$^2$ needs a current density of 90 mA m$^{-2}$ (assumed). The rectifier output voltage is 10 V. Find the current, the electrical power and the yearly energy.

steps.text: Total current is the area times the current density.

blocks.answer: 16.2 A, 162 W and about 1419 kWh per year.

blocks.markdown: **Marine structures: zones.** A steel pile in the sea passes through different environments. In the **atmospheric zone** a high-performance coating system (epoxy primer with polyurethane topcoat) is used. The **splash and tidal zone**, wetted intermittently and exposed to oxygen, abrasion and wave impact, suffers the most severe attack and cathodic protection works poorly there because the surface is often out of the electrolyte, so heavy-duty coatings or sheathing are used. In the **submerged zone** coating plus cathodic protection is standard: the coating cuts the current demand and the CP protects the bare spots, while pitting and crevice attack at joints and bolts must be designed out.

rows: Atmospheric
Salt-laden air; uniform rusting and coating failure
Multi-coat paint system, regular maintenance
Splash and tidal
Wet-dry cycling, oxygen, abrasion; the most severe corrosion
Heavy-duty coating, sheathing or corrosion allowance
Submerged
Seawater electrochemical corrosion, pitting at defects
Coating plus sacrificial or impressed-current CP
Buried in sediment
Low oxygen but bacterial action possible
CP (current demand lower than in water)
blocks.caption: Protection chosen zone by zone.

blocks.title: Cathodic protection is not a cure for every form
blocks.text: Cathodic protection stops anodic attack only where current reaches the metal in the electrolyte. It does not protect surfaces out of the water, it can cause hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steel and disbond coatings if the potential is too negative, and stray current from an impressed system can damage neighbouring structures.

points: Uniform corrosion thins the whole surface, pitting makes isolated deep cavities, crevice corrosion is confined to a gap and stress-corrosion cracking gives fine cracks needing tensile stress, a specific environment and a susceptible alloy.

Sacrificial anodes need no power but are consumed and limited in current; impressed-current systems use inert anodes and a rectifier and suit large, long-life structures but need control to avoid overprotection.
A marine steel structure is protected zone by zone: coatings above water and in the splash zone, coatings plus cathodic protection when submerged, and careful detailing of joints.

questions.stem: Inspection of a type 316 stainless steel tank wall that held a warm chloride brine shows a scatter of small isolated holes up to 3 mm deep, while the flat surface between them is bright and almost unmarked. Which form of corrosion is this?

options.text: Uniform corrosion
Stress-corrosion cracking
Pitting
Crevice corrosion confined to a gasket

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: uniform corrosion would thin the whole surface evenly.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: SCC gives fine cracks with little metal loss, not cavities.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: isolated deep cavities with the surrounding surface almost unattacked are the signature of pitting.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: crevice attack lies inside a gap; here the holes are on an open, flat surface.

questions.explanation: Chloride breaks down the passive film at isolated points, and each point becomes a small anode with a large cathode around it, so the cavities deepen while the rest of the surface stays bright. This differs from crevice attack, which needs a gap, and from SCC, which needs tensile stress and produces cracks.

questions.stem: On a stainless-steel flange joint exposed to seawater, damage is found only underneath a rubber gasket and around the bolt washers, while the open flange faces are in good condition. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Crevice corrosion, because oxygen is depleted and chloride and acidity build up in the stagnant gap
Uniform corrosion, because the whole joint is exposed to seawater
Stress-corrosion cracking, because the bolts are tightened
Pitting caused by the flow velocity of the seawater over the flange faces

questions.correctOptionText: Crevice corrosion, because oxygen is depleted and chloride and acidity build up in the stagnant gap

distractorRationale.a: Correct: attack confined to a narrow stagnant gap is crevice corrosion.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: uniform attack would also affect the open faces.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: SCC would show as fine cracks and requires a specific tensile-stress and environment combination.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the open faces are unattacked, so the damage is tied to the gap rather than to flow.

questions.explanation: In a gap the electrolyte is stagnant, oxygen is used up and cannot be replaced, and dissolving metal makes the local solution acidic and chloride rich, which sustains and accelerates the attack. The open faces keep a passive film because oxygen reaches them freely.

questions.stem: A brass cartridge case that was cold-formed and stored in an atmosphere containing traces of ammonia develops fine branching cracks with almost no metal loss. Which conditions are necessary for this form of failure?

options.text: Only a corrosive environment, because stress is not needed for cracking
Only a tensile stress above the yield strength of the metal
A large cathode area compared with the anode area
A tensile stress, a specific corrosive environment and a susceptible alloy acting together

questions.correctOptionText: A tensile stress, a specific corrosive environment and a susceptible alloy acting together

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: stress is essential; without tensile stress there are no cracks.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: SCC occurs at stresses well below the yield strength, including residual stress from forming.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the area ratio governs galvanic attack, not the cracking mechanism.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: all three conditions are needed; removing any one prevents stress-corrosion cracking.

questions.explanation: Stress-corrosion cracking, here the classic season cracking of brass, needs residual tensile stress from cold forming, an ammonia-bearing environment and a susceptible alloy. Annealing to relieve residual stress or excluding the environment removes the cause.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares sacrificial-anode and impressed-current cathodic protection?

options.text: An impressed-current system needs no external power because its anodes corrode spontaneously
A sacrificial system needs no external power but its anodes are consumed, whereas an impressed-current system uses an external rectifier and inert anodes
A sacrificial system has adjustable current output controlled by a rectifier
Both use inert anodes, differing only in the electrolyte

questions.correctOptionText: A sacrificial system needs no external power but its anodes are consumed, whereas an impressed-current system uses an external rectifier and inert anodes

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: an impressed-current system must have an external DC power supply.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: this states the defining difference between the two systems.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the current of a sacrificial anode is set by its potential difference and cannot be adjusted by a rectifier.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: sacrificial anodes are active metals that are consumed, not inert.

questions.explanation: A sacrificial anode (zinc, aluminium alloy or magnesium) is more active than steel, so it dissolves and supplies protective current without any power source. An impressed-current system supplies current from a rectifier through inert anodes, so output can be adjusted but power and monitoring are needed.

questions.stem: A steel offshore structure is coated and also has sacrificial anodes in the submerged zone. Why is the coating used together with cathodic protection rather than cathodic protection alone?

options.text: The coating replaces the need for any protective current
The coating makes the anodes more active so they corrode faster
The coating prevents the anodes from reacting with seawater
The coating cuts the current demand so the anodes last longer and fewer are needed

questions.correctOptionText: The coating cuts the current demand so the anodes last longer and fewer are needed

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: coatings contain defects, so some protective current is still needed.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the coating does not change the anode activity; faster consumption would shorten life.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: anodes must contact seawater to work; the coating protects the steel, not the anodes.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: current is needed only where the coating is broken, so the demand and anode mass fall sharply.

questions.explanation: Bare steel in seawater needs a current density of order 100 mA per square metre, but the coated area needs only a small fraction of this, set by the breakdown factor. Coating and CP therefore complement each other, giving longer anode life for a given mass.

questions.stem: A steel coupon loses mass equivalent to an average penetration of 0.25 mm over a test period, while the deepest pit found is 1.5 mm deep. Calculate the pitting factor $d_{\max}/d_{\text{avg}}$. Give a dimensionless number.
questions.explanation: The pitting factor is $d_{\max}/d_{\text{avg}}=1.5/0.25=6.0$. A value well above 1 indicates localised attack: the worst penetration is six times what mass loss alone would suggest.

questions.stem: A coated structure has $A=800$ m$^2$ of surface, a coating breakdown factor of 0.03, and bare steel demands 120 mA m$^{-2}$. It is protected by 250 kg of aluminium-alloy anodes with a capacity of 2500 A h kg$^{-1}$ (typical) and a utilisation factor of 0.9. Calculate the anode life in years (1 year = 8760 h).
questions.explanation: The current demand is $I=800\times0.03\times0.120=2.88$ A, and the usable charge is $250\times2500\times0.9=5.625\times10^{5}$ A h. Life is $5.625\times10^{5}/2.88=1.953\times10^{5}$ h, which is $1.953\times10^{5}/8760=22.3$ years.

questions.stem: An impressed-current system protects a bare steel jetty with a submerged area of 150 m$^2$. The design current density is 110 mA m$^{-2}$ (assumed) and the rectifier operates at a steady 8 V. Calculate the electrical energy used in one year of continuous operation (8760 h), in kWh.
questions.explanation: The current is $150\times0.110=16.5$ A and the power is $8\times16.5=132$ W. Over 8760 h the energy is $132\times8760/1000=1156$ kWh.

questions.stem: Compare sacrificial-anode and impressed-current cathodic protection for a steel structure. Include how each works, the advantages and drawbacks of each, and the circumstances in which each is the better choice.
markingGuide: Principle: both make the structure the cathode and move its potential to a protective value (for steel in seawater about -0.80 V against Ag/AgCl)
Sacrificial: an active metal (Zn, Al alloy, Mg) corrodes instead of the steel; no power needed; simple; current fixed by the potential difference; anodes are consumed and must be replaced
Impressed current: an external DC rectifier drives current from inert anodes; the output is adjustable and large; needs power, monitoring and maintenance
Drawback of impressed current: overprotection can disbond coatings or cause hydrogen embrittlement in high-strength steel; stray currents can harm neighbouring structures
Selection: sacrificial for small or well-coated structures or remote sites; impressed current for large structures, long life or high-resistivity electrolytes
questions.explanation: Both systems supply electrons to the structure to suppress anodic dissolution, but they differ in the source of current. The choice rests on size, life, access to power and the cost of maintenance.

questions.stem: Specify a corrosion-protection scheme for a steel pier in a marine environment, with different zones: atmospheric, splash/tidal and submerged. Justify the method in each zone and describe one detailing precaution against a localised form of corrosion.
markingGuide: Atmospheric zone: high-performance coating system (for example epoxy primer plus polyurethane topcoat), with maintenance
Splash/tidal zone: most severe attack with wet-dry cycling; CP is ineffective when the surface is out of the electrolyte, so heavy-duty coating, sheathing or corrosion allowance
Submerged zone: coating plus cathodic protection (sacrificial anodes, or impressed current for a large pier), with the coating reducing the current demand
Mentions the protective potential criterion (about -0.80 V against Ag/AgCl) or the need to monitor it
Detailing: avoid crevices at joints and bolts (seal or weld), avoid sharp stress concentrations or residual stress where SCC is possible, and avoid pit initiation sites
Considers overprotection risk or galvanic effects of dissimilar metals
questions.explanation: A good scheme matches each method to the zone where it works: coatings where the surface is intermittently wet, and cathodic protection where the structure is continuously immersed. Detailing prevents the localised forms that protection alone cannot stop.
